title: driver/run.json (where a driven session's loop is, and why it stopped)
description: The current state of one driven session, under .dabbler/runs/s<N>/driver/run.json. Written only by `dabbler session drive`, replaced whole after every transition, and read by a re-run to continue where the last one left off: the phase, the steps already accepted, the tree the next report is measured against, the seq last issued and the invocations spent. It is state, not history -- the history of a run is its transcripts and the lifecycle's own records. `stop` is the one field a person is meant to read: when the loop halts short of the close it says which bound it met, in words, and a re-run clears it. A file that fails validation on read is refused, never skipped. `rejections`, `job` and `engine_session_id` are optional for exactly that reason: they arrived with the pull, and a run written before them is still a run this reader must open.

schema_version.description: Frozen at v1. A reader that finds any other value refuses the file rather than interpreting it.

engine.description: The adapter the engine is reached through, by name. A re-run with a different one is refused: one engine's session store carries the run.

phase.description: Where the loop is. A re-run enters here; `complete` means the close ran and nothing is left to do.

seq.description: The seq of the instruction last issued, so the next one is monotonic across re-runs.

invocations.description: How many times the engine has been invoked for this session, across re-runs. On a seat each one is a premium request.

max_invocations.description: The bound `invocations` is held under. Reaching it stops the loop and closes nothing; continuing is a re-run with a larger bound, which is a decision to spend more.

accepted_steps.description: The work-plan steps whose reports were accepted, in order. A re-run skips them.

baseline_tree.description: The tree object the working tree was at after the last accepted step, which is what the next report's `files_changed` is measured against. Null before the first step.

kind.description: Which bound the loop met: the invocation budget; a step refused three times; the engine reporting `blocked`; the engine failing to run; a test run the framework could not hand back; a verification round that neither passed nor produced findings to dispose; the commit or push; the close's gates; a person asking it to stop (`session interrupt --stop`, with their reason).

stop.description: Null while the loop runs or after it completed. Set when it halted short of the close, with the reason in words; the session stays in flight and this is what the operator reads.

rejections.description: How many times the outstanding answer has been refused, out of the three a step is allowed. It is here rather than in a local because a pull-mode call -- `dabbler session next` -- ends between the refusal and the answer, and a count a process holds is a count that resets every time the person's CLI comes back.

name.description: What the framework is running, in the words the instruction shows: a verification round, a suite's run of record, the close.

argv.description: The program and its arguments, spawned with no shell.

log.description: Where the job's output is being appended, repository-relative -- the path a `wait` hands back.

status.description: The file the runner writes the exit code into when the job ends, repository-relative. Its presence is what tells a finished job from a running one; a pid alone cannot, because pids are reused.

job.description: The one long-running thing the framework has started and has not yet collected, or null. Long work is never awaited inside a call: a verification round, the complete suite and the close each outlast an engine's tool timeout, so they are started detached and the following call reports progress or the result.

engine_session_id.description: The engine's own conversation, by the id it reported on its first invocation. A resume names it; nothing here asks an engine for its most recent session, because the most recent one in a directory can be somebody else's.
